---
title: "Part 2 – The claim, its estimand and its causal graph"
---
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Slides.** [Open the deck at this part](../../slides/trust-one-day.html#/part-2-the-claim-its-estimand-and-its-causal-graph){target="_blank"} in its own tab, or follow it on the [slides page](slides.qmd).
:::

Part 2 is the conceptual middle of the day. It reads the paper, sets out what the five Multi100 analysts did with its claim, and argues that analysts who look as though they disagree are often answering different questions. It then gives you two tools for saying which question you are answering, the estimand statement and the causal graph, and uses both on the claim, where the graph asks what each control of the paper is: a common cause of concern and distrust, a step on the path between them, or a consequence of both.

| Work through | What you do | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Slides, Part 2 | The paper of the original author (OA): the question that it asks, the data and the measures, the association between and within countries, the model and its result, and the claim as SCORE selected it, with the ellipsis that removes the clause about the controls. | 16 minutes |
| Slides, the five analysts | The five Multi100 analysts placed by their coefficients, then a table of what each of them did: one verdict, and estimates that differ by a factor of two. | 6 minutes |
| Slides, the estimands run | Two studies set beside our five: the red-card estimates again as a single row, the four estimands that the twenty-nine teams were in fact pursuing, and the spread that collapses once the estimand is fixed. Then what under-specified research questions mean for the reading of many-analysts studies, and the steps from a theoretical to an empirical estimand that Lundberg and colleagues set out. | 12 minutes |
| Slides, the causal-graph crash course | Confounders, mediators and colliders; the causal stories that can lie behind one correlation; open and closed paths; total against direct effects; selection and feedback. | 14 minutes |
| Slides, the claim | The estimand statement, which everyone writes in chat, holds and sends together; the causal graph of the claim; what holding the controls of the paper constant does in that graph; the three readings of the far-right vote and the verdict on public services; and why no set of controls can settle reverse causation. | 16 minutes |
| Slides, the R tutorial | Optional, if the class wants it: R in one slide, reading and inspecting the data, the verbs that work on rows and columns, scales from items, model formulas with fixed and random intercepts, a plot, causal graphs in R, and the error messages that you are most likely to meet. | 8 minutes |
| Task 2 in your report or working script, or [Browser lab](../../cases/trust/lab.qmd#task-2-data) Task 2, with [Causal graphs and adjustment sets](../../companion/dags.qmd) as the slower companion | Count the respondents, the countries, the country-rounds and the respondents of the paper; compute Cronbach's alpha for the three immigration items; compare the correlation of concern with distrust across the country means and within the countries. Write the estimand statement with every bracket filled, saying which institution and what you hold constant. Then open `R/dag_starter.R`, take the `#` off the arrow from concern to distrust if you believe it, run `adjustmentSets(dag)`, `paths(dag, Z = paper_set)` and `isAdjustmentSet(dag, paper_set)`, and try the two swaps that the file offers. Finish with two sentences: what holding the controls of the paper constant does in your graph, and whether any set of controls can tell an effect of concern from an effect of distrust. | 18 minutes |

**By the end of the part** you have the estimand behind the claim written in one sentence, a graph that includes only the arrows you are willing to defend, and two sentences on what the controls of the paper do to the comparison and what no control can do.
